common_name: Carolina White Rice (Historic Lowcountry Sister to Carolina Gold)

planting.note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–May for an August–October harvest. Carolina White can be grown in standard garden beds kept consistently saturated rather than true flooded paddies, though paddy conditions give the highest yields.

directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Carolina White was the pale-hulled sister landrace grown alongside gold-hulled Carolina Gold throughout the antebellum South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry, part of the same rice culture built on enslaved West African agricultural expertise that made Charleston one of the wealthiest colonial ports. Like Carolina Gold, Carolina White nearly vanished after the Civil War and through the collapse of Lowcountry rice culture in the early 20th century; the two landraces are close kin, and rice geneticists working with the Carolina Gold Rice Foundation and Anson Mills have noted that recovered Carolina Gold populations can express Carolina White characteristics. Grow it exactly as Carolina Gold — in a saturated bed or shallow paddy — and expect a tall, long-grained rice with a milder, less golden husk color but similar exceptional cooking quality. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain hardens, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling.

planting.note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Toro was developed at the LSU AgCenter Rice Research Station near Crowley, Louisiana, as a specialty long-grain with the clingy cooked texture normally associated with short- and medium-grain rice.

directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Toro is a specialty long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter Rice Research Station near Crowley, bred with low amylose content and a low gelatinization temperature that give the cooked grain a soft, clingy, jasmine-like texture despite its long-grain shape — unlike the fluffy, separate-grain texture of standard American long-grain rice. Unlike aromatic Louisiana specialty rices such as Della and Jazzman, Toro carries no distinctive fragrance; its value is purely in cooking texture, making it popular for dishes and cuisines that call for a stickier grain. The tall plants perform well through the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain turns golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before storage or milling.

common_name: Blue Rose Rice (Historic Louisiana Short-Grain, Sol Wright's Red-Rice-Resistant Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Blue Rose was selected in 1907 near Jennings, Louisiana, by breeder S.L. (Sol) Wright specifically to grow clean of red rice contamination in Gulf Coast paddy fields.

directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Blue Rose is one of the most historically important American rice varieties: Louisiana breeder S.L. (Sol) Wright selected it in 1907 from Japanese rice grown near Jennings, Louisiana, specifically to resist the red rice contamination that was devastating the milled quality of the era's crop, and released it commercially in 1911. Blue Rose went on to dominate American rice production for more than 25 years — by 1934, roughly three-quarters of all rice grown in the United States traced to Wright's Blue Rose breeding work, and Louisiana State Rice Milling sold it as its flagship short-grain product under the Water Maid brand. The short-to-medium grain mills cleanly and cooks up tender, making it well suited to jambalaya, dirty rice, and other Cajun and Creole one-pot dishes that favor a softer grain. The historic site of Wright's original selection in Crowley is preserved today at Crystal Rice Heritage Farm. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain hardens, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling.
